intro: A week about attention: a derivation, a quiet film, Sakamoto's last concert, a room turned into a camera, and a few good puzzles. Pick what calls to you.

items.title: Derive why attention divides by the square root of d
items.description: Scaled dot-product attention computes softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)). Derive where the sqrt(d_k) comes from, then predict what goes wrong without it.
items.why: A one-line design choice you use every day. Deriving it trains the habit of asking what a scale factor protects against.
steps: Assume each component of q and k is independent with mean 0 and variance 1. Compute the mean and variance of q.k.
Show that dividing by sqrt(d_k) brings the variance back to 1, whatever d_k is.
Take logits with large variance and write down what softmax does to them. Then write the softmax gradient and see what happens to it.
Check your answer against footnote 4 of the Transformer paper.
Bonus: if q and k come from LayerNorm with a learned gain, which assumption breaks, and does the fix still hold?
hints: q.k is a sum of d_k products. Each product has mean 0. What is the variance of one product?
Variances of independent terms add. So the variance of the sum grows with d_k.
Large logits push softmax towards one-hot. Look at the Jacobian diag(p) - pp^T when p is almost one-hot.

resources.title: Attention Is All You Need
resources.creator: Vaswani et al.
resources.note: The original argument is two sentences long. Compare it with your derivation.

items.then: Explain to a friend in two minutes why a bigger head size needs a smaller logit scale.

items.title: Removal or suppression? Design the test for an unlearning claim
items.description: A paper says its method makes a model forget a set of facts, and accuracy on those facts drops to chance. Design the smallest set of experiments that would tell you whether the knowledge was removed or only hidden.
items.why: Many evaluation claims fail on exactly this question. Designing the control yourself is the core skill of critical reading.
steps: Write down two hypotheses: the knowledge is gone, or it is still there but suppressed at the output.
For each hypothesis, list what you would expect from probes on hidden states, a few steps of fine-tuning on related data, and rephrased or translated prompts.
Add an anchor: a model that never saw the facts. Say what each test should show for that model.
Pick the three tests that best separate the hypotheses for the least compute.
Compare your design with the methods in the Lynch et al. paper and with the anchors paper on this week's reading list.
hints: Accuracy at the output only tells you about the output. Where else could the information live?
If a few gradient steps on unrelated but nearby data bring the facts back fast, what does that say?
A model trained without the facts is your ground truth for 'absent'. Every test needs a target value from it.

resources.title: Eight Methods to Evaluate Robust Unlearning in LLMs
resources.creator: Lynch et al.
resources.note: A checklist of attacks that recover supposedly forgotten knowledge.

resources.title: Compared to What? Calibrating Machine-Unlearning Diagnostics with Present, Absent and Suppressed Anchors
resources.note: This week's reading list. Read it after you have your own design.

items.then: Write your three tests as a short reviewer comment, as if the paper were under review.

items.title: From residual connections to hyper-connections, and why mHC lives on the Birkhoff polytope
items.description: Hyper-connections replace the single residual stream with several streams that mix at every layer. DeepSeek's mHC keeps training stable by forcing the mixing matrix to be doubly stochastic. This week's trending cmHC paper asks how much mixing is right.
items.why: The residual stream is the backbone of every Transformer and of most interpretability work. This is a live change to it, with clean maths underneath.

explain.what: A family of architectures where the residual path becomes n parallel streams mixed by learned matrices.
explain.why: Plain residuals trade off gradient flow against representation collapse. Several streams with learned mixing aim to get both.
explain.how: At each layer a small matrix mixes the streams. mHC projects that matrix onto the set of doubly stochastic matrices using Sinkhorn iterations, so the mixing cannot blow up or shrink the signal.
components: Sinkhorn projection onto doubly stochastic matrices
a mixing trade-off between independent streams and identical streams
explain.limitations: Extra memory traffic for n streams. Gains are mostly reported at large scale, so small reproductions may not show them.
explain.research_relevance: Changes what 'the residual stream' means, which matters for probing, steering and circuit analysis.

steps: Read the Hyper-Connections abstract and Section 2. Draw the n-stream picture for n = 2.
Read the mHC method section. Write why a doubly stochastic matrix keeps the average signal size fixed.
Read the Sinkhorn paper's Section 4 to see how alternating row and column normalisation works.
Read the cmHC abstract and its mixing trade-off. Ask what too little and too much mixing would look like in a probe.
Do this week's maths question on doubly stochastic matrices alongside.

resources.title: Sinkhorn Distances: Lightspeed Computation of Optimal Transportation Distances
resources.creator: Marco Cuturi

resources.title: cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction

items.then: Write three sentences on what a 'residual stream direction' means when there are four streams.

items.subject: maths
items.title: Why is every doubly stochastic matrix an average of permutations?
items.description: A doubly stochastic matrix has non-negative entries and every row and column sums to 1. The Birkhoff and von Neumann theorem says each one is a weighted average of permutation matrices. Prove it, or at least see why it must be true.
items.why: It turns a messy set of matrices into a clean polytope whose corners are permutations. It is the geometry behind mHC, optimal transport and matching problems.
hints: Start with 2 by 2. Write the general doubly stochastic matrix with one free number t and spot the two permutations.
For the general case, draw a bipartite graph with an edge wherever the entry is positive. Why does Hall's marriage condition hold?
A perfect matching gives a permutation P. Subtract c times P, with c the smallest matched entry. What is left, and what has dropped?
Induct on the number of positive entries.

resources.title: Doubly stochastic matrix
resources.note: Statement and context. Try the proof before reading.

resources.title: A Short Proof of the Birkhoff von Neumann Theorem

cross_domain.connection: The corners of the Birkhoff polytope are permutations, so mHC's mixing matrices are literally blends of ways to shuffle residual streams.

items.subject: probability
items.title: Bertrand's paradox: what is a 'random chord'?
items.description: Draw an equilateral triangle inside a circle. Pick a chord of the circle at random. What is the chance it is longer than a side of the triangle? Joseph Bertrand showed in 1889 that three reasonable methods give three different answers. Find all three, then decide which one, if any, is right.
items.why: 'At random' hides a modelling choice. The same trap appears whenever a paper samples 'random' prompts, inputs or directions.
hints: Method one: fix one end of the chord and pick the other end uniformly on the circle.
Method two: pick a random radius, then a uniform point along it, and draw the chord perpendicular to the radius there.
Method three: pick the chord's midpoint uniformly inside the disc. Which midpoints give long chords?
E. T. Jaynes asked which answer stays the same if you shift or rescale the circle a little. Which method survives that test?

resources.title: Bertrand's Paradox (with 3blue1brown)
resources.creator: Numberphile
resources.note: Watch after you have your three numbers.

items.then: Name one place in ML evaluation where 'random' quietly hides a choice like this.

items.subject: physics
items.title: Why does a spinning phone flip around one axis but not the other two?
items.description: Toss your phone (over a bed) spinning about each of its three axes. About the long axis and the flat axis it spins cleanly. About the middle axis it flips half a turn every time. In 1985 the cosmonaut Vladimir Dzhanibekov saw a wing nut do this in orbit. Why is the middle axis unstable?
items.why: A result you can feel in your hands and then prove with three equations. It is a clean example of stability analysis, the same tool used for training dynamics.
steps: Do the experiment first. Note which axis flips.
Order the moments of inertia I1 < I2 < I3 and match them to your phone.
hints: Write Euler's equations for a free rigid body with no torque.
Suppose the spin is almost all about one axis, with tiny wobbles about the other two. Linearise.
You get a second-order equation for a small wobble. Its sign decides oscillation or exponential growth. Check the sign for each axis.
For a picture without equations, think about energy and angular momentum both being conserved. Where do those two surfaces meet?

resources.title: The Bizarre Behavior of Rotating Bodies, Explained
resources.creator: Veritasium

items.subject: physics
items.title: If hot air rises, why is it cold on top of a mountain?
items.description: Hot air rises, the Sun heats the whole atmosphere, and a mountaintop is closer to the Sun. Yet it is colder up there, by roughly 6 to 10 degrees per kilometre. Explain why using only the first law of thermodynamics and the fact that pressure falls with height.
items.why: A two-line argument that overturns a common intuition. It also explains clouds, snowlines and why mountain winds can be warm.
hints: A rising parcel of air moves to lower pressure. What does it do to its surroundings as it expands?
Air is a poor conductor, so the rise is close to adiabatic. Where does the energy for the work come from?
Try to estimate the dry lapse rate as g divided by the specific heat of air at constant pressure. Then ask why real air cools more slowly than that.
items.then: Use it to explain a warm, dry wind coming down the far side of a mountain range.

items.title: The Great Stink of 1858: right fix, wrong theory
items.description: In the hot summer of 1858 the Thames, full of London's sewage, smelled so bad that Parliament finally acted. Joseph Bazalgette built a network of intercepting sewers and the Embankments to carry waste downstream. Cholera in London largely stopped. But most leaders backed it because they believed disease spread through bad air, not dirty water.
items.why: A great conversation story with a research lesson inside: a correct intervention justified by a wrong model. John Snow had already linked cholera to water in 1854.
steps: Read the London Museum story on the summer of 1858.
Then read how Bazalgette built the sewers.

resources.title: A very smelly summer in the city: the Great Stink of 1858
resources.creator: London Museum

resources.title: How Bazalgette built London's first super-sewer
resources.creator: London Museum

cross_domain.connection: A fix that worked for the wrong reason. Good results do not prove the theory behind them, in 1858 or in an ablation table.

items.then: Question to discuss: what modern policy or method might be working for reasons we have wrong?

items.title: How undersea cables carry the internet, and why they became geopolitics
items.description: Almost all intercontinental internet traffic runs through a few hundred fibre-optic cables on the seabed, not satellites. They land at a small number of coastal stations and pass through chokepoints like the Red Sea. Recent cable cuts in the Red Sea and the Baltic have made them a security issue, and big tech companies now fund many new routes.
items.why: Explains a recurring news thread: why a ship's anchor or a regional conflict can slow the internet across a continent, and who owns the pipes.
steps: Open the 2026 Submarine Cable Map. Find the cables that land in your country and count the landing points.
Trace a route from South Asia to Europe. Note every chokepoint it passes.
Read TeleGeography's short post on how many cables exist.
Optional: the introduction of The Undersea Network for why cables land where they do.

resources.title: How Many Submarine Cables Are There, Anyway?
resources.creator: TeleGeography

items.then: Next time the news mentions a cable cut, you will know which map to open.

items.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto: three pieces and his last concert
items.description: Sakamoto moved from electronic pop to film scores to spare solo piano. Listen to three pieces, then watch Opus, a black-and-white film of him playing alone, made by his son Neo Sora shortly before his death in 2023.
items.why: One musician's life in three pieces. It also pairs well with the Japanese lessons and with this week's quiet film.
steps: Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence (1983): the theme from the film he also acted in. Listen for how one simple melody carries both warmth and distance.
Energy Flow (1999): a short piano piece that became a surprise hit. Notice how little happens and how calm it feels.
Aqua (from the album BTTB, 1998): listen for the left hand, which keeps moving like water under a still surface.
Watch Ryuichi Sakamoto | Opus in one sitting, ideally with good headphones and the lights low.

resources.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto: Coda
resources.creator: Stephen Nomura Schible
resources.note: If you want his life story afterwards.

items.then: Pick the one piece you would play for a friend, and say in one sentence why.

items.title: Vilhelm Hammershøi: two quiet rooms to look at slowly
items.description: The Danish painter Hammershøi (1864 to 1916) painted the same few rooms of his Copenhagen flat again and again: grey walls, closed doors, light on the floor. Spend ten minutes each on two works: Dust Motes Dancing in the Sunbeams (1900), an empty room crossed by light, and Interior with Young Woman Seen from the Back (1904).
items.why: Slow looking is a skill. These paintings reward it because almost nothing is in them, so you start to see light, edges and silence.
steps: Open Dust Motes Dancing in the Sunbeams full screen. For five minutes, only follow where the light goes.
Ask what an empty room with only light in it makes you feel, and why.
Then look at Interior with Young Woman Seen from the Back. What do you feel about a person whose face you never see?

resources.title: Vilhelm Hammershøi 1864-1916
resources.creator: Ordrupgaard
resources.note: The museum that owns Dust Motes Dancing in the Sunbeams.

resources.title: Sunbeams or Sunshine. Dust motes dancing in the sunbeams
resources.creator: Vilhelm Hammershøi

items.then: This week's camera obscura is a good follow-up: it is a room like his, painted by light.

items.title: Perfect Days: a film about paying attention
items.description: Wim Wenders' 2023 film follows Hirayama, who cleans public toilets in Tokyo. He reads, listens to old cassettes and photographs the light through trees. Koji Yakusho won Best Actor at Cannes for the role. Almost nothing happens, and that is the point.
items.why: It is the vision of Northstar as a film: a narrow, chosen life full of noticing. It also shows everyday Tokyo, useful for your Japanese.
steps: Watch it without a phone nearby.
Notice how the same day repeats and what changes each time.
Stay for the end card that explains the Japanese word komorebi.

resources.title: Wim Wenders and Yakusho Koji take film to the toilet with Perfect Days
resources.creator: nippon.com

items.then: Take one photo of komorebi, sunlight through leaves, this week.

items.title: Ted Chiang's Story of Your Life: linguistics, physics and free will
items.description: A linguist learns an alien written language and it changes how she experiences time. The novella, the basis of the film Arrival, uses Fermat's principle of least time from optics as its key idea: light seems to 'know' its destination before it leaves.
items.why: Few stories make real physics and real linguistics carry the emotion. It is also a beautiful way into variational principles.
steps: Read the novella in one or two sittings. It is about 60 pages.
When Fermat's principle appears, pause and draw the light bending at a water surface.
Afterwards ask whether a language could really change how you think about time, and what linguists say about that idea.

resources.title: Stories of Your Life and Others
resources.creator: Ted Chiang

resources.title: Story of Your Life
resources.note: Background only. Read after the story, it has spoilers.

cross_domain.connection: Fermat's least-time principle describes light by its whole path, not step by step. The story asks what a mind that saw the world that way would feel.

items.title: Loop before you reply, in one real conversation
items.description: Looping is a listening technique used by mediators. You say back what you heard in your own words, then ask 'Did I get that right?', and keep going until the other person says yes. Only then do you reply.
items.why: People rarely feel heard, even by good listeners. Looping makes understanding visible, and it slows you down before you argue.
steps: Pick one conversation this week where the other person cares about what they are saying: a disagreement, a worry, or an idea they are excited about.
After they finish a point, say 'So what I am hearing is...' in your own words, including how they seem to feel.
Ask 'Did I get that right?' If they correct you, loop again.
Only after a clear yes, give your own view.
items.then: Afterwards, notice whether the conversation changed after the first 'yes, exactly'.

items.title: Homework for Life: find one story a day, tell one
items.description: Matthew Dicks, a many-time Moth storytelling winner, suggests spending five minutes each evening noting the most storyworthy moment of the day, however small. By the weekend, pick one and tell it to someone in under a minute.
items.why: Good conversationalists are not more interesting people. They notice small moments and know how to shape them.
steps: Each evening, write one line: the moment from today that you would tell if you had to tell one.
On Saturday, pick the best one. Find the moment where something changed.
Tell it to a friend or family member in under 60 seconds, starting as close to that change as you can.

resources.title: Storyworthy
resources.creator: Matthew Dicks
resources.chapters: The chapter on Homework for Life

resources.title: A Budding Storyteller Turns In His Homework for Life
resources.creator: WBEZ

items.then: Keep the best story. You now have one ready for the next quiet moment at dinner.

items.title: Turn a room into a camera obscura
items.description: Black out a room on a sunny day and make a small hole in the cover over the window. The street outside appears upside down on the opposite wall, in colour and moving. The photographer Abelardo Morell has turned rooms around the world into cameras like this.
items.why: It is the oldest camera, and it still feels like magic. You learn how every camera and eye works by standing inside one.
steps: Choose a room with a window facing something bright. Cover the window fully with cardboard or foil and tape.
Cut a hole about 1 cm across. Wait five minutes for your eyes to adjust.
Hold a white sheet a metre from the hole, then move it. Watch focus and brightness change.
Try a smaller hole and a bigger one. Note the trade-off between sharpness and brightness.
Take a long-exposure phone photo of the wall.

resources.title: Friday DIY: Create Your Own Camera Obscura
resources.creator: Getty Museum

resources.title: Abelardo Morell and the Magic of the Camera Obscura
resources.creator: SFMOMA

cross_domain.connection: A smaller pinhole cuts geometric blur but adds diffraction blur, so there is a best size. It is a bias and variance style trade-off you can see on a wall.

reflection_prompt: Optional: which item made you notice something you usually walk past?

lessons.title: Introduce yourself: hajimemashite, desu, yoroshiku
lessons.explanation: A Japanese self-introduction has three parts. Start with はじめまして (hajimemashite), 'nice to meet you for the first time'. Say your name and add です (desu), which works like 'I am' and keeps it polite. End with よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu), which means roughly 'please treat me kindly'. A small bow fits naturally at the end.

examples.text: AIのけんきゅうをしています。
examples.romanization: AI no kenkyuu o shite imasu.

examples.text: しゅみはどくしょです。
よろしくおねがいします。
examples.meaning: Pleased to meet you. (literally: please treat me well)

questions.question: How do you say 'Nice to meet you. I'm Kenji.'?
questions.answer: はじめまして。ケンジです。 (hajimemashite. Kenji desu.)

questions.question: What do you say at the end of a self-introduction?
questions.answer: よろしくおねがいします。 (yoroshiku onegaishimasu.)

questions.question: Fill the gap: しゅみは ___ です。 'My hobby is music.' (music = おんがく, ongaku)
questions.answer: しゅみはおんがくです。 (shumi wa ongaku desu.)

questions.question: Someone says はじめまして、タナカです。 What do you reply?
questions.answer: はじめまして、(your name)です。よろしくおねがいします。

practice: Say your own four-line introduction out loud three times: hajimemashite, your name desu, one fact, yoroshiku onegaishimasu.
Record yourself once and listen back for the long 'uu' in kenkyuu and the soft 'r' in yoroshiku.
Role-play meeting someone new with Claude: Claude introduces itself first, then you reply.

resources.title: Jikoshoukai: how to introduce yourself in Japanese
resources.creator: Tofugu

lessons.title: Hello, your name and how are you, politely
lessons.explanation: Telugu has a polite 'you', మీరు (mīru), and an informal one, నువ్వు (nuvvu). Use mīru with anyone you don't know well or who is older. Polite verbs for 'you' often end in -āru, as in ఉన్నారు (unnāru), 'you are'. 'Your' is మీ (mī) and 'my' is నా (nā).

questions.question: How do you ask an older person 'How are you?'
Which word for 'you' is polite: నువ్వు (nuvvu) or మీరు (mīru)?
Someone asks మీరు ఎలా ఉన్నారు? Reply 'I'm fine, and you?'

practice: Say the full exchange out loud five times: namaskāram, ask the name, give yours, ask how they are, answer.
Practise the retroflex ṭ in ēmiṭi: curl the tongue tip back a little.
If you know a Telugu speaker, greet them with namaskāram and mīru elā unnāru this week.
